answer.rationale: P99 latency spike of 5x target coinciding with a release 2 hours ago strongly suggests the new build introduced a regression. Memory_b1 shows rollback cleared a checkout error spike cleanly without customer impact; memory_b6 shows staged gating catches regressions early. The write path degradation during settlement peak (heavy transactional load) is the highest-risk scenario for customer impact. Rollback is the fastest path to restore latency stability while preserving all in-flight writes—we revert to the prior stable build and re-evaluate the release offline. This also preserves uncertainty: if the release is innocent, we'll have telemetry from the rollback to guide our next decision. Given settlement traffic is at peak and we have capacity for only one intervention, rolling back eliminates the most acute risk vector (the unknown change that shipped 2 hours ago) without requiring the latency recovery time of failover or the operational complexity of adding capacity mid-incident. Small guarded test scale allows us to validate rollback safety on a subset before full fleet if needed, though given memory_b1 precedent, we can execute with high confidence.
